articles.title: A JSONB Side Table Only Wins on Rows You Rewrite Twice
articles.description: I have a table that holds issue reports. Each row has a few fields that change all day (a status, a...
articles.body_html:
I have a table that holds issue reports. Each row has a few fields that change all day (a status, a counter, a timestamp) and one big JSONB column holding the whole issue body. The status flips every time someone triages an issue, the body almost never changes, and the write-ahead log on that database had started to feel like the most expensive part of the whole setup. A reader, johnnylemonny, left a comment on my last piece about JSONB under write load, and his point was blunt: do not split the hot fields into a side table. The big payload already lives outside the row in TOAST, he said, so an update that only touches the hot fields rewrites a narrow tuple with an 18-byte pointer where the payload used to be. The side table would save almost nothing and charge you a second insert, a second primary key index, and a join on every read.

I believed him. Almost. The reasoning is clean, and clean reasoning about databases has a way of being right right up until you measure it. So I measured it: same workload, two shapes, two payload sizes, everything twice. One thousand rows, hot fields updated in scattered rounds the way a real triage queue updates them, and the log measured before and after each batch so every number below is bytes that actually got written.

My claim before the numbers: the side table is not a saving. It is a bet on how often you rewrite the row. And like most bets, it pays on some rows and loses on others, and the payload size decides which.

Problem 1: HOT fires everywhere, and that changes the whole argument

The first surprise is how completely HOT wins. Across the eight cells, 7,996 of 8,000 hot-field updates were HOT updates, every cell at 99.9 percent or better. No index maintenance, no new index entries, just a new tuple version on the same page. That needs two things to be true: the columns you change are not indexed, and the page has free space. I gave the tables room with a fillfactor of 80, and I updated rows scattered across the table instead of sweeping the whole thing in one go.

That second detail matters more than it looks. My first attempt swept all 1,000 rows in a single update, and HOT fired only about a quarter of the time, because rewriting every row on a page burns through its free space in one pass. Scattered writes are what a live queue actually does, and under scattered writes HOT is not a sometimes thing. It is the whole story. If your hot fields are indexed, or your pages are packed full, none of what follows applies, and that is the first thing to check before you believe any number in this piece, including mine.

Problem 2: with a small payload, the split wins by a lot

When the payload is small, about 170 bytes, it stays inside the row. Then the in-table shape pays for it on every update: 368 bytes of log per hot-field update, because each new tuple version carries the payload along. Move the payload to a side table and the same update costs 150 bytes. That is a 218-byte saving per update, about 59 percent, and it is the only cell where the split looks like an obvious win.

But the split charges rent. Inserting a row now costs 513 bytes of log instead of 334, the extra insert plus its primary key index. Divide one by the other and the break-even is under one update per row: 179 bytes extra on the insert, 218 saved on each update. Any row that gets rewritten even once has paid for the split. Most rows in a triage queue get rewritten more than once, so for small inline payloads the side table is a fair trade, and the argument against it mostly fails.

Problem 3: with a big payload, TOAST does most of the work, not all of it

This is the cell johnnylemonny was actually arguing about, and he was mostly right. When the payload is about 8,180 bytes of real text, it spills out of the row into TOAST (five thousand toast chunks across my thousand rows), and the in-table hot update drops from 368 bytes to 231. The pointer really is cheap. The whole point of his comment survives the measurement: the scary version of this story, where every status flip rewrites eight kilobytes of issue body, does not happen. HOT plus TOAST already killed it.

Where his comment goes too far is the word "matching." The in-table update costs 231 bytes and the side-table update costs 151. The side table still wins, by 80 bytes per update, about 35 percent. The tuple version in the main table is still wider than the slim side row, pointer or not. Eighty bytes is not much, and on the insert side the split still charges its 182 bytes, so the break-even moves to about two and a quarter rewrites per row. But it is not zero, and "the split saves nothing" is the kind of clean claim that only survives until someone measures it. He reasoned from the mechanics. The mechanics said the pointer is 18 bytes. The measurement says the row around the pointer still costs you.

Problem 4: the insert is the payload, wherever you put it

The least surprising number is also the one that kills the most arguments. Inserting a row with an eight-kilobyte payload costs about 9,054 bytes of log in the table and 9,236 in the split shape. The payload has to be written once, wherever it lives, and TOAST writes it either way. The split adds 182 bytes to a nine-thousand-byte operation. If you were hoping the side table would make inserts cheaper, it will not, in either size: for the small payload the split makes inserts more expensive, and for the large one it makes them trivially more expensive. The split is a tax on writes that create rows and a discount on writes that change them. Whether that trade is good depends on your ratio of creates to rewrites, and nothing else.

Reads, for completeness: a thousand point lookups took between 0.12 and 0.29 seconds in both shapes, and the spread between my two repetitions was bigger than any gap between the shapes. At this size there is no join tax worth quoting. On a bigger table, with colder caches, there might be. This run cannot tell you that, and I am not going to pretend it can.

Problem 5: the run I threw away

I should say plainly that my first version of this run measured the wrong thing. The "large" payload I built was eight thousand copies of the same letter, and Postgres compressed it down to 173 bytes inside the row, so nothing ever spilled to TOAST and both sizes measured the same small thing. Real issue bodies do not compress fifty to one. I rebuilt the payload out of hundreds of different hashes so it would not compress, confirmed five thousand toast rows, and ran everything again. The numbers above are the second run. The lesson is boring and worth writing down: a test payload has to behave like the real data, and repeating characters do not.

The other honest limit: these are a thousand rows on one machine, hot fields unindexed, pages given room. Change any of that — an indexed status column, the default fillfactor, a vacuum that cannot keep up — and HOT stops firing, and the in-table shape gets expensive in exactly the way this piece says it does not. The numbers are real. Their range is narrow.

So the rule I am keeping is simple enough to fit on a sticky note. If the payload stays inline, split when rows get rewritten at all. If the payload spills to TOAST, split only when a row gets rewritten more than twice. And if a row is written once and never touched again, do not split it: you are paying an insert, an index, and a join for a discount you will never collect.

johnnylemonny's comment was the reason this piece exists, and he was right about the mechanism and wrong about the size of the saving, which is the best kind of comment to get. Where do you draw the line in your own tables — do you split hot fields out, or do you trust HOT and leave the row alone? And if you have measured it rather than reasoned it, what did the log actually say?

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Push Is Attention. Pull Is the Correctness Floor
articles.description: rudratosh left a comment on my last piece that I have been turning over for two days. The piece was...
articles.body_html:
rudratosh left a comment on my last piece that I have been turning over for two days. The piece was about a slow payment confirmation: my helper sent a $29 charge, the reply took 2.5 seconds, and my helper's own patience ran out after 1 second, so it wrote the step down as UNKNOWN even though the money had already moved. The fix was a claim row, a small record that says who owns this delivery and whether it finished, and the planner reading that row before it plans anything. One delivery, no duplicate, no second charge.

rudratosh asked the next question, and it was the right one. Reading the row works. But what about being told? What if something watches the row and taps the planner on the shoulder the moment the late reply lands, instead of the planner going to look? Does that change the next plan any differently? And what happens when the tap lands in the middle of a step, or arrives twice, or arrives after the planner has already stopped?

I spent a night testing it on the same small setup, with the same $29 payment and the same slow receiver. Three versions of the same evening, and the answer surprised me in one place and confirmed my guess in another.

Problem 1: the tap lands mid-step, and the step does not care

Here is the shape of the test. The planner has three steps: deliver the payment, send the customer confirmation, report the result. The payment goes out, the reply takes 2.5 seconds, and after 1 second the planner already believes the step is UNKNOWN. At 2.5 seconds the reply lands and the claim row flips to done. A watcher sees that flip and drops a note into the planner's inbox: version 2, status done.

But step 1 is not finished at 2.5 seconds. It still has a second and a half of follow-up work, drafting the confirmation note. So the tap lands mid-step, at about 3 seconds in, while the step is still working.

What should the planner do? My first instinct, a month ago, would have been to stop everything and re-plan on the spot. The test says that instinct is wrong, and rudratosh said the same in his follow-up comment: finish the step, then re-read before the next one. The step already in flight has its own delivery key and its own duplicate protection, so letting it finish is safe. Yanking it halfway just creates a second half-finished piece of work to clean up, and now you have two messes instead of one.

So that is what the test planner does. It finishes step 1 at 4.5 seconds, drains its inbox at the boundary, sees the newer version, reads the row again, and plans step 2 on the fresh fact. One delivery. No re-send. The mid-step tap changed nothing about the step in progress, and that is exactly the point.

Problem 2: the tap that arrives twice looks like news

Halfway through step 2, the watcher delivered the same note again. Version 2, status done, second copy. In a real system this happens all the time: a watcher retries, a queue redelivers, a tired network sends the same thing twice.

Without a version number, the second copy looks like a brand new event. The planner would read the row again for no reason, or worse, treat it as a second change and start second-guessing a plan that was already right.

With the version number, the test is boring, and boring is good. The planner compares the token against the last version it read that turn. Token 2 against last seen 2: equal, so it is a duplicate, ignored. The inbox file holds four lines (versions 1, 2, 2 again, 3), and the planner's log says, in plain words, that the second copy was a duplicate and it moved on. The version number is what turns a redelivery from an event into noise.

This is the part people skip when they build a notification channel and call it done. A push without a version is a rumor. A push with a version is a fact you can check.

Problem 3: the flag that must forget

Here is the subtle one, and rudratosh pushed me on it twice. The planner keeps a small flag: a newer version exists than the one I cached, so my cache is stale. A token sets the flag. The planner re-reads the row at the next boundary. Then what? Does the flag stay dirty until the turn ends, or does it clear?

It clears on the re-read. The flag is an edge, not a level. Its whole meaning is "there is a newer row than the one you cached," and once you have re-read and refreshed, that job is done. Leaving it dirty forces a pointless re-read at every later boundary, and worse, it hides the next token. If token 3 lands after the re-read, you want the flag to flip again and earn its own re-read. A flag that never clears cannot tell you anything twice.

But the clearing itself has a trap, and this is where I had to write a separate test, because the live run never caught it. Between "read the row" and "clear the flag" there is a gap, and a token can land in that gap. If the planner clears the flag with a plain reset, the new token is lost: the flag reads clean although a newer row exists.

The fix is to clear by comparing: only clear if the flag still holds the token you actually read. I tested both ways against the same timing. The compare-and-swap clear refused and kept token 3 dirty. The plain reset cleared it and lost token 3. Same setup, same timing, opposite results. It is a five-line difference, and it is the difference between a planner that notices the second change and one that sleeps through it.

Problem 4: the planner is already dead

The last test was the ugliest. I killed the planner after step 1 and then let a change arrive: an outside note on the claim row, version 2 to 3, token 3, at 5.4 seconds. The watcher saw the planner's heartbeat go stale, checked that the process was gone, and sent the note somewhere else: a fallback owner's file, not the dead inbox.

The dead inbox still holds the two notes from when the planner was alive, versions 1 and 2, unread. Nobody will ever read them. That is fine. What matters is that the post-death note went to a human-shaped destination instead of vanishing into a queue nobody drains. A push channel with no living receiver is a letter to an empty house. Somebody has to own the fallback, or the observation is lost exactly when it matters most — right after something died.

Problem 5: push and pull gave the same answer, so why push at all?

Here is the result that made me sit back. Pull and push reached the same next plan. One delivery each, no duplicate, proceed to step 2. The log-only version, where the fix existed but nobody read it, sent the payment twice.

So push changed nothing about the decision. The planner learned earlier, mid-step instead of at the planning moment, but it decided the same thing, on the same row. That is rudratosh's point, and the test backs him: push is attention only. It tells you when to look. Pull is the correctness floor. It is what you look at. If the push ever disagrees with the row, the row wins, every time, because the row is the state and the push is only a rumor about the state.

So why build push at all? Because attention has a price in the other direction. A planner that only pulls learns late. In my test the planner's patience ran out at 1 second and the reply landed at 2.5. A planner that pulls only at planning time sits on a wrong belief for the whole gap, and if the next step starts before the pull, it re-sends a payment that already went through. Push shortens that gap. It does not make the decision better. It makes the decision sooner, and sooner is worth something when the wrong decision costs $29 twice.

That is my claim, and I know it is arguable: a notification that changes when you look is worth building, but it is never worth trusting. The row is the truth. The tap is only the tap on the shoulder. If you build the tap and skip the row, you have built a faster way to be wrong.

Have you ever had a system where the notification arrived and the state said something different? Which one did you trust, and what did it cost you? I would like to hear what it was, and whether you still trust the tap now or read the row first every time.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: How an emptyDir With medium: Memory Made Our Export Pods OOMKilled While the Heap Sat at 210 MB
articles.description: Our report-export pods died with exit code 137 every few hours, but the Node heap never passed 210 MB against a 1 GiB limit. The missing memory was a tmpfs scratch volume that Kubernetes bills to the container
articles.body_html:
02:47 UTC, Wednesday. PagerDuty: reports-export restarts > 3 in 30m. I open the Kubernetes dashboard and the restart counter on the deployment reads 17. Last reason for each one: OOMKilled, exit code 137.

the scramble

Three of us end up in the channel. The export service builds CSV and XLSX files for enterprise customers, and the on-call for the finance team says three scheduled month-end exports are missing. Customers are asking where their files are.

First theory, from everyone at once: memory leak in the last release. It shipped on Monday and added a new XLSX writer. That fits the timeline, so I start there.

It stops fitting quickly. The container limit is 1 GiB. I pull the Node heap metrics we export from process.memoryUsage() and the heap never crosses 210 MB on any pod, including the ones that were killed. RSS is 340 MB at the last scrape before each death. A leak in the new writer would show up as a climbing heap, and it is a flat line.

the hunt

Dead end one: native memory. Streaming XLSX libraries sometimes buffer in Buffers outside the V8 heap. That would show in RSS, and RSS is 340 MB. Still nowhere near 1 GiB.

Dead end two: the kernel log. I read the node's dmesg for the OOM kill record, expecting to see a process using 1 GiB of anonymous memory. The record is there, and it is odd:

memory: usage 1048576kB, limit 1048576kB, failcnt 8841 Memory cgroup stats for /kubepods/burstable/pod4c1e.../a7f3...: anon 351068160 file 12582912 shmem 702545920 Killed process 29114 (node) total-vm:1204816kB, anon-rss:338120kB

anon is 335 MB, which matches the Node process. shmem is 670 MB. Something holds 670 MB of shared memory inside this container's cgroup, and it is not our code's heap.

Shared memory in a container is usually /dev/shm or a tmpfs mount. I check the pod spec and find it. When the platform team enabled readOnlyRootFilesystem in September, the export service lost the ability to write to /tmp, so somebody added a scratch volume:

volumes: - name: scratch emptyDir: medium: Memory containers: - name: reports-export volumeMounts: - name: scratch mountPath: /tmp resources: limits: memory: 1Gi

medium: Memory backs the volume with tmpfs. I exec into a live pod and run df -h /tmp. It reports 4.2 GB size (half the node's RAM, since no sizeLimit was set) and 640 MB used, with 22 leftover files from earlier exports.

The exporter writes each finished file to /tmp/exports/<job-id>.xlsx, uploads it to S3, and deletes it. Except the delete only runs on the success path. Any job that failed the upload, which happens a few times a day when the S3 call times out, leaves its file behind. Those files are in RAM, and tmpfs pages are charged to the memory cgroup of the container that wrote them.

So the heap graph was a decoy. Every dashboard we had measured the process. The kernel measures the container, and ours had a RAM disk in it.

the find

Month-end is when the large exports run. A single 180 MB XLSX plus the pod's baseline 340 MB is fine. But the S3 timeouts cluster at month-end too, because the same batch hammers the bucket. Each failed upload strands another 150 to 200 MB file in tmpfs. Four stranded files, one new export in progress, and the cgroup hits 1 GiB. The kernel cannot reclaim tmpfs pages (there is no swap), so it kills the process.

One more detail made the incident look like a leak: emptyDir lives as long as the pod, not the container. When the OOM killer restarted the container, the stranded files were still there, so the replacement started its life already carrying them. That is why restarts bunched up instead of clearing the problem.

To confirm, I delete the stranded files from one pod by hand and watch it. Its memory working set drops from 910 MB to 330 MB and it stops restarting. A second pod I leave alone is killed again at 03:31.

the fix

Two changes. First, the scratch volume goes back to node disk, with an explicit size cap and an ephemeral-storage limit so the kubelet evicts instead of the kernel OOM-killing a healthy process:

volumes: - name: scratch emptyDir: sizeLimit: 2Gi containers: - name: reports-export resources: requests: ephemeral-storage: 1Gi limits: memory: 1Gi ephemeral-storage: 2Gi

Second, the code now cleans up on every path, and on startup it wipes anything left in the scratch directory from a previous container:

async function runExport(job) { const path = \\\`/tmp/exports/\\${job.id}.xlsx\\\`; try { await buildWorkbook(job, path); await uploadToS3(path, job.key); } finally { await fs.rm(path, { force: true }); } } // at boot await fs.rm('/tmp/exports', { recursive: true, force: true }); await fs.mkdir('/tmp/exports', { recursive: true });

I also added a 30-second timeout and two retries on the S3 upload, which is what had been producing the stranded files in the first place.

the aftermath

  • Impact: 17 restarts across 5 pods between 22:10 Tuesday and 03:40 Wednesday, and 3 month-end exports delayed by about 4 hours. The jobs were re-run from the queue, so nothing was lost.
  • Alert added: container working_set_bytes divided by limit, plus a separate panel for container_memory_cache and shmem, so a gap between heap and container memory is visible in one place.
  • A policy check in CI now rejects medium: Memory on any emptyDir without a sizeLimit and a note about what the memory limit has to cover.
  • Runbook line: if OOMKilled and the process heap is flat, read shmem in the cgroup stats before looking for a leak.

A RAM-backed volume makes a file feel free, and it isn't: it draws from the same 1 GiB as the heap. We spent two hours hunting a leak in code that was fine, while the memory that mattered was sitting in a directory.

articles.title: I Wish I Could See Your ChatGPT History.
articles.description: If you really wanted to understand how someone thinks, would you rather read a hundred of their...
articles.body_html:
If you really wanted to understand how someone thinks, would you rather read a hundred of their answers or a hundred of their questions?

I think I'd choose the questions.

Sometimes, when I come across a particularly impressive developer on GitHub, I find myself wondering what their ChatGPT history looks like. Not because I'm interested in how much of their code was written by AI, but because I'm curious about the things they don't understand.

There's something rather comforting about the possibility that someone whose work I find incredibly sophisticated might have spent an entire afternoon struggling with something I happen to find simple.

Of course, if someone were to direct that same curiosity towards my conversation history, they would probably find some very entertaining things.

But it has made me think about how little we actually know about the way other people learn, particularly now that so much of our learning happens in conversations nobody else gets to see.

Learning to code in the age of AI

I'm currently in my third year of engineering, which puts me in a rather interesting generation of developers. By the time I seriously entered software development, generative AI was already available. I never really had to rely on Stack Overflow in the way that many experienced developers describe having done.

For me, AI wasn't a disruption to an established way of learning. It was part of how I learned in the first place.

I can ask a question without necessarily knowing how to articulate it. I can interrupt an explanation because something halfway through doesn't make sense. I can ask the same question three different ways and, occasionally, discover that what I thought I was confused about wasn't actually the source of my confusion.

I sometimes wonder what those experiences would have looked like had I started programming ten years earlier.

Perhaps some of my questions would have ended up on a public forum. Someone might have responded, someone else might have disagreed, and years later, another student struggling with the same thing might have stumbled across that conversation.

Instead, most of my questions have served exactly one person: me.

There's every possibility that someone somewhere has spent an evening trying to understand the exact same thing I have, made the same incorrect assumptions, and eventually arrived at the same understanding through a remarkably similar conversation with AI.

We could have had quite an interesting conversation with each other.

Instead, we both closed our respective chat windows and moved on.

I wouldn't necessarily call that a bad thing. The accessibility of personalised technical help is something I wouldn't willingly give up. But I do find it fascinating that two people can share an almost identical learning experience without ever knowing the other exists.

How strange it is to look at someone else's GitHub

One of my favourite ways of discovering new technologies is looking through other people's projects. Unfortunately, it's also a remarkably efficient way of discovering several new reasons to feel behind.

I'll come across someone my age working with a technology I've barely heard of, follow a few links, and somehow end up with another five things on my already unreasonable list of things to learn.

What I rarely consider in those moments is that somebody looking through my work might be doing exactly the same thing.

They might see a machine learning project I've built and assume that I'm comfortable with everything that went into it. They wouldn't know which concepts took me several attempts to understand, which decisions I reconsidered, or which seemingly straightforward parts turned out to be unexpectedly difficult.

And, naturally, I don't know any of that about them either.

I think there's an interesting imbalance in how we experience our own competence compared to everyone else's. We have access to every moment of our own confusion, but relatively few moments of anybody else's.

AI conversations have made that imbalance even more pronounced. Much of the questioning, experimenting and misunderstanding that goes into learning something can now happen entirely in private.

The resulting project, however, is still public.

It would be interesting to know how differently we might perceive each other if we could see even a small fraction of what happened before that project appeared on GitHub.

The questions that never make it into a commit

One thing I've found particularly amusing about learning software development is how inconsistently knowledge seems to accumulate.

You can understand something relatively sophisticated and remain completely unfamiliar with something supposedly fundamental. You can spend weeks working with a technology and still discover something about it that makes you wonder how you managed to use it for those weeks.

Just recently, somewhere among my conversations about software development and machine learning, I asked ChatGPT what Registry Editor in Windows was.

I rather enjoy the fact that these questions coexist.

Technical knowledge doesn't seem to organise itself according to the difficulty levels of a programming course. We encounter things as they become relevant to us, develop oddly specific areas of expertise, and sometimes discover fairly elementary gaps much later than we might have expected.

A résumé has very little room for that nuance. Neither does a GitHub profile.

But I've also noticed that some of the most valuable time I spend learning doesn't necessarily result in anything I can put on either of them.

Sometimes, something is already working, and I simply want to understand why. I might spend another hour reading about it, questioning an implementation or following a line of curiosity that has little practical relevance to the project anymore.

At the end of that hour, there might be no new code to commit. The application works exactly as it did before.

The only thing that has changed is my understanding of it.

I find it interesting that, in a profession where we have so many ways of making our progress visible, this particular kind of progress is almost impossible to see from the outside.

It probably exists somewhere in a conversation titled something extraordinarily unhelpful, like "Explain this."

Perhaps the questions are worth sharing, too

I've been thinking about starting a technical blog for a while, and I kept returning to the question of what I knew enough about to write.

I could explain an algorithm, write about a framework, or put together a tutorial. But whenever I considered doing that, I found myself wondering what would make someone want to read my explanation when they could already get a perfectly reasonable one from an AI.

The things I find most interesting about other developers are often considerably more personal than their explanations of technology. I'm curious about why they chose to build something, what surprised them along the way, which assumptions they had to reconsider, and what they ended up being curious about afterwards.

I would particularly love to know what they found difficult. Not because it diminishes anything they've accomplished, but because it gives me a much richer understanding of the person behind the accomplishment.

Perhaps that's something we could afford to share a little more often.

And perhaps, rather than waiting until I've understood something well enough to write about it, I could occasionally write about the experience of trying to understand it.

I'm twenty, and I imagine my thoughts about software engineering will change considerably over the next few years. I'll probably revisit some of what I write here and wonder how I ever arrived at those conclusions.

I'm rather looking forward to that.

It would be nice to have somewhere on the internet where I could return, years from now, and recognise the person I was while learning all of this.

Somewhere other than my ChatGPT history.

articles.title: One VM, 15 Million Web Servers: The Per-Socket Tax Your Kernel Charges
articles.description: How many web servers can one virtual machine hold? Not how many requests it can answer per second, and not how many containers you can squeeze onto it, but some
articles.body_html:
How many web servers can one virtual machine hold? Not how many requests it can answer per second, and not how many containers you can squeeze onto it, but something more literal: how many servers can each open a socket, listen on their own address, and answer a request, all at the same time?

A writeup published this week by kapteko asked exactly that question under a hard budget: one VM, ten gigabytes of RAM, one CPU core, and a target of fifteen million web servers. It reads like a joke whose punchline is fixing the economics of hacking by making servers too abundant to attack, but underneath the humor sits one of the clearest public walkthroughs of what the Linux kernel actually charges you for networking, and what it costs to stop paying. Every wall the experiment hits is a wall that real systems hit later and rename as an outage.

Wall one: the kernel runs out of ports

The experiment starts with the smallest honest web server you can write in C: create a socket, listen, accept, read, reply, close.

int main(void)
{
    int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (listen(server, 128) < 0)
        return 1;
    const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK";
    for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) {
        if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0)
            send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        close(client);
    }
}

On one core this loop answers around 65 thousand requests per second, which sounds like a fine start. Then the experiment tries to launch fifteen million copies and dies at copy number 28,232. The failure is not CPU or memory. It is listen returning an error, because each server asked for port zero, and the kernel assigns those from net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, which defaults to 32768 through 60999. That is roughly 28 thousand ports, and the experiment just exhausted every one of them.

Widening the range to the full 1 through 65535 space buys only about 64 thousand more, because a port is a sixteen-bit field baked into the TCP header itself. No sysctl stretches a protocol constant. The real escape hatch is a different observation: a listening socket is identified by the tuple of protocol, IP address, and port, so fresh addresses multiply the port space for free. Linux supports exactly this through a feature called AnyIP, which lets one machine listen on an entire routed subnet:

sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo

A single /64 prefix is about 18 quintillion addresses, which is generous headroom. The IPv4 equivalent is theoretically identical and practically awkward, since a routable block with fifteen million addresses trades at roughly a quarter of a billion US dollars these days. Address space, not silicon, is the scarce resource.

Wall two: every socket costs 3,384 bytes, even idle

With addressing solved, the next question is memory, and here the experiment catches a widely repeated claim being wrong. Ask a language model how much RAM an idle TCP connection takes and it will answer confidently: zero for idle, about five kilobytes for active. The experiment believed this, allocated fourteen million idle listening sockets, and watched the machine run out of memory almost immediately.

The truth is visible in the kernel source. A single TCP socket on Linux carries roughly 3,384 bytes of bookkeeping before one byte of user data moves. struct tcp_sock alone is 2,240 bytes of state for queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, and retransmit accounting. socket_alloc adds 768 bytes for the socket object and its sockfs inode. The file structure costs 184 bytes, and the dentry for the pseudo-filesystem name costs 192. None of this is a buffer you can tune away with sysctl; it is the price of the kernel remembering that your socket exists.

Multiply by the target and the math turns brutal: fifteen million kernel sockets need about 48 gigabytes of RAM, five times the whole budget, before any server answers a single request. In the configuration the experiment actually measured, the stock networking path ran the machine dry at roughly 2.5 million servers, with throughput decaying well before that point.

Wall three: a process per server is worse

Even with free sockets, the classic Unix design would still lose. A minimal compiled server process costs about 1.5 megabytes of RAM, so fifteen million of them would need on the order of twenty terabytes. The only way forward is the move language runtimes made years ago: put every guest inside one process and schedule them yourself.

The writeup builds this on LFI, a sandboxing scheme from Stanford research that gives each guest memory isolation and, crucially, replaces every syscall with a call into the host runtime. That replacement is the whole trick: once the kernel is no longer involved in guest I/O, the runtime can implement networking however it wants. The machine becomes its own tiny operating system, with a scheduler that round-robins between guests.

How small can per-guest state get? Look at the server loop again. Between any two scheduling points, the only live values are the program counter and two file descriptors:

struct Context {
    pc: u64,        // where to resume
    fd_server: i32, // listening socket
    fd_client: i32, // current client
};

Sixteen bytes per guest, and less if you pack aggressively. Fifteen million guests of scheduling state fit in about 220 megabytes. Combine that with the corrected memory model — fourteen million idle connections held inside a userspace stack, one million active connections at five kilobytes each — and the total lands near five and a half gigabytes: just over half the budget. The plan survives contact with arithmetic. Now it has to survive contact with the network card.

Wall four: TCP has to leave the kernel

TCP is the stateful part of the stack; everything below it is stateless framing, so nothing forces the TCP implementation to live in the kernel. Embedded engineers have carried their own stacks for decades, and Adam Dunkels famously shipped Miniweb, a TCP/IP stack plus HTTP server that runs in twenty-eight bytes of RAM. Mature options exist at every weight class: gVisor reimplements the entire operating system interface including networking, Seastar ships a full runtime with its own stack, lwIP is the classic C implementation, and F-Stack ports the FreeBSD stack wholesale.

The experiment picks smoltcp, a standalone event-driven TCP/IP stack written in Rust for bare-metal systems. The choice is well supported: the crate needs no heap allocation, carries a 0BSD license, sits at roughly 4.7 thousand GitHub stars, and shipped release v0.14.0 in August 2026 with commits still landing this month. But smoltcp is deliberately only the protocol half. It parses and emits packets; it cannot move one byte to the wire by itself. You feed it through a device abstraction:

loop {
    let now = Instant::now();
    iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets);
    wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?;
}

Everything interesting hides inside what device is.

Feeding the stack: TUN, TAP, DPDK, AF_XDP

There are four realistic ways to connect a userspace stack to the wire, and they differ in how much of the kernel you keep paying for.

TUN is a virtual kernel interface at the IP layer; TAP does the same job at the Ethernet layer. Both are easy — smoltcp supports them out of the box — but packets still cross the kernel boundary on every trip, so the per-syscall and per-copy costs remain.

DPDK removes the kernel from the data path entirely. The application talks to the network card through memory-mapped ring buffers: sending is writing to memory, receiving is reading memory the card already filled. Context explains why anyone bothers. A syscall costs on the order of 500 nanoseconds, and a kernel-to-userspace copy perhaps another 1,000, while a trading firm saturating a 400-gigabit link must process up to 600 million packets per second — 1.7 nanoseconds per packet. At that budget you cannot afford to even ask the kernel a question. The catch is operational: the poll loop pins an entire core at one hundred percent, and the DPDK driver takes exclusive ownership of the card. The interface vanishes from ifconfig, and if that card carried your SSH session, the session is gone.

AF_XDP is the modern middle path. The kernel keeps owning the device, but a small eBPF program attached at the XDP hook decides per packet whether to redirect the frame straight into a userspace memory region — bypassing the whole network stack — or hand it to normal processing. The region is managed as receive and transmit descriptor rings per socket, plus fill and completion rings over a shared UMEM buffer, which yields zero-copy I/O while SSH, monitoring, and every other kernel consumer keep working. A SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL mode trades a core for interrupt-free polling when you want behavior even closer to DPDK. For smoltcp specifically, the rust-dpdk-net and xsk-rs crates already wrap the two fast paths, so the device trait is the only glue left to write.

What the final benchmark says

The writeup closes with the comparison the whole piece builds toward. The kernel path dies around 2.5 million servers when RAM runs out. The userspace path slows memory growth to about 620 bytes per idle server and roughly one kilobyte per active one, which is how the experiment finally passes its target: sixteen million web servers, alive, on ten gigabytes. On throughput, DPDK wins the benchmark outright with AF_XDP close behind — the expected result, since AF_XDP keeps a thin slice of kernel involvement that DPDK does without. The full proof of concept, including the scheduler, the LFI plumbing, and all four network backends, is public in the author's AI10M repository.

What this buys you at normal scale

Nobody needs fifteen million web servers. But the per-socket tax applies at every scale: a million idle WebSocket or SSE connections — ordinary for a chat product or a mobile backend — cost about 3.4 gigabytes of kernel memory before your application does anything at all. Knowing that number changes how you argue about architecture. Connection-heavy services can budget for the tax explicitly, move idle state out of the kernel with a userspace stack on the hot path, or adopt AF_XDP where operations teams cannot hand a network card to a single process. The joke experiment turns out to be a measurement of a price most of us pay without ever reading the receipt.

Originally published on Dispatch.

articles.title: I Trimmed My Agent's Tool Results to Five Fields. It Solved More, Not Fewer.
articles.description: A reader named izgorodin left a comment on my piece about the 200-tool menu, and it changed the...
articles.body_html:
A reader named izgorodin left a comment on my piece about the 200-tool menu, and it changed the question I thought I was answering. He had run the numbers himself: forty turns of a triage helper whose only tool returns five GitHub issues, and by turn twenty the tool results were 99.1 percent of everything sent, about 326,000 tokens, thirteen times the cost of the menu itself. Keeping only the last six turns flattened the call at around 99,000. Trimming each result to the five fields the helper actually reads kept the whole history and ended turn forty at 36,934. Then he wrote the sentence that matters: his replay called no model and used a fixed answer, so it measured how big the window gets, not whether the helper still finds what it needs.

That is the question I spent this week answering. Same twelve triage jobs, run twice: once with the full issue text coming back, once with each result cut to the five fields (the number, the title, the labels, the comment count, and the first 300 characters of the body). A real model did the work, a small one I run locally, and every job was scored on whether it found the right issue and the right label. I expected the trim to cost something. I was wrong about the direction.

My claim before the numbers: trimming the results would save about half the tokens per turn and cost a few solved jobs, because sooner or later the helper would need something the trim cut. The first half was right. The second half was backwards.

Problem 1: the trim did not cost a single solved job

Across both runs, the full results solved 9 of 24 jobs. The trimmed results solved 17 of 24. That is 37.5 percent against 70.8, and the gap is not a rounding error in one direction: the trim won 9 to 4 in the first run and 8 to 5 in the second. Look at the twelve jobs one by one and the trim never loses a job the full text wins. The two arms agree on seven jobs (both solve four, both fail three), and on the other five the trim wins or ties every time.

Three jobs beat the model in both arms, and they are worth naming because they set the limit. On the Linux dependency guide, the Windows 11 question, and the misspelled error dialog, the model answered the crash-on-launch issue every single time, in both arms, in both runs. Those are small-model limits, not trim damage. The trim cannot be blamed for what the full text also fails, and the fact that the failures are identical in both arms is the cleanest evidence in the whole run that the trim is not hiding anything load-bearing.

Problem 2: the full text has a favourite issue, and it is always the crash

The full arm's failures have a shape, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. On five of its failed jobs, the model answered issue 412, the crash on launch, with the label "bug" — whatever the job actually asked. The job about garbled dates in a CSV export? 412, bug. The job about the install guide missing a Linux step? 412, bug. The job about a typo in an error dialog? 412, bug. It even went back and read 412 a second time before answering it, as if checking its work.

The trimmed arm does the same second look just as often, about once per job in both arms, but it answers the right issue afterwards. The difference is not that the trim hides the crash report. It is that five short results sit side by side and all five stay visible, while five long ones let the most dramatic report swallow the rest. A small model reading a long list does not weigh five issues. It remembers the loudest one. Cutting the noise did not just save tokens. It changed what the model could pay attention to, and attention was the scarce thing, not information.

Problem 3: the full text can eat the whole window just by looping

The ugliest full-arm result is not a wrong answer. It is no answer at all. On two jobs the model listed the issues, listed them again, and listed them again, six turns of the same call, and burned 10,063 tokens on one job before the turn cap stopped it. The first time I ran this, that loop pushed the prompt past the model's whole window and the run died outright. I added a rule that a repeated call comes back as a one-line note instead of the full dump again, the same rule in both arms, and the run survived, but the loop still cost the job.

The trimmed arm never needed a fourth turn on any job. Every job ended in three: list, one second look, answer. The full arm averaged close to four turns and needed six on its worst jobs, and each of those extra turns carried another thousand-plus tokens of history with it. The token bill per turn tells the same story from the other side. Turn one is identical in both arms, about 179 tokens. Turn two is 1,749 with full results and 759 trimmed. By the third turn the full arm is sending about 1,900 tokens a turn and the trimmed arm about 1,080. The average across the run is 1,421 tokens per turn against 673, and 5,475 per job against 2,020. The trim cuts the bill by more than half per turn and almost two thirds per job, and the jobs it saves are the ones where the full text was already losing.

Problem 4: the second look is not the price of the trim

izgorodin asked for a miss signal alongside the solved rate, and he was right to: a trim that quietly sends the helper back for the full text every time has not saved anything, it has just moved the cost. So I counted every time the helper asked for one issue in full. Full results: 0.88 second looks per job. Trimmed results: 0.92. That is the same number, inside the wobble between runs, and it is the number that surprised me most. The trim did not drive the helper back for more. The helper goes back about once per job in both arms, usually to look once more at the issue it is about to answer, and the full text costs the same second look for the same reason.

That kills the natural objection in both directions. The trim is not free because the helper never needs the cut material: it goes back just as often. And it is not expensive because of the second looks, because the second looks cost the same either way. The saving is in the list itself, paid once per turn, and the second look is a fixed cost of doing the job carefully, not a tax on trimming.

Problem 5: the honest limit is the size of the model

All of this is one small model on twelve jobs. A bigger model would solve more jobs in both arms (the three jobs that beat this one in both arms would probably fall), and the gap between the arms would likely shrink. The absolute rates, 38 percent and 71 percent, belong to this model and these twelve jobs, and anyone quoting them as general truths about agents is over-reading a small run. Twelve jobs is also small enough that the run-to-run wobble is a whole job per arm. I ran it twice for that reason, and the direction held in both runs, but the direction is the finding, not the percentages.

The other limit is the jobs themselves. My issue bodies run a hundred-odd words, shorter than real reports. Real bodies are longer, messier, and more repetitive, which would widen the token gap, not narrow it. But it would also give the trim more to cut, and I have not measured that. The five fields are also izgorodin's five, chosen for a triage prompt that cites numbers and suggests one existing label. A different prompt reads different fields, and its trim would cut somewhere else.

So the rule I am keeping is narrower than the one I went in with. Trim the result to the fields the prompt actually reads, and measure the solved rate before you argue about it, because the cost you expect (the helper going back for what you cut) may not exist, and the benefit you did not expect (the helper deciding better with less noise) may be the whole story. The menu was never the bill. The results were. And the results, it turns out, were also the distraction.

What do you trim from your tool results, and did you check whether the solved rate moved when you did? I would like to hear the number, either way, and what the helper went back for when it went back.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: TypeScript `Const` Assertions on Function Arguments in 2026: When Inline `as const` Beats a Generic Constraint
articles.description: Inline as const on function arguments preserves literal types without generic constraints. Learn when to apply const assertions at the call site versus encoding them in the function signature.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript Const Assertions on Function Arguments in 2026: When Inline as const Beats a Generic Constraint

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers preserve literal types by adding generic constraints to function signatures. This forces every caller to satisfy the constraint, even when the function does not need narrower types. The function signature grows complex, and callers lose flexibility. When a route definition function demands a constraint like T extends readonly string[], teams must decide whether that constraint belongs in the signature or at the call site.

TypeScript 3.4 introduced const assertions with as const syntax (documented in the TypeScript 3.4 release notes), allowing developers to freeze literal types at the expression level. When applied inline to function arguments, as const narrows the type at the call site without changing the function signature. The function accepts the widened type, but the caller supplies a narrowed literal that TypeScript preserves through inference.

This pattern shifts type narrowing from the function's responsibility to the caller's control. The function signature stays simple. Callers who need narrow types add as const. Callers who prefer flexibility omit it. Teams avoid encoding every type requirement in the function signature itself.

Key Takeaways

  • Inline as const on function arguments preserves literal types without changing the function signature, shifting narrowing control from function author to caller.
  • Generic constraints like T extends readonly string[] force every caller to satisfy the constraint even when the function logic works with widened types.
  • Applying as const at the call site allows the function to accept both wide and narrow types, with callers choosing which behavior they need.
  • Combining const type parameters (<const T> syntax in TypeScript 5.0+) with inline assertions provides granular control over which arguments narrow and which stay flexible.
  • Inline as const breaks type inference when the compiler cannot unify the narrowed type with the function's expected parameter type, requiring explicit type annotations to resolve.

Why Generic Constraints Fall Short for Literal Preservation

Generic constraints enforce type boundaries but do not preserve literal specificity. A constraint like T extends string accepts both "GET" and string, yet the function's return type sees only the constraint's upper bound. The literal information vanishes.

function defineRoute<T extends string>(method: T) {
  return { method };
}

const route = defineRoute("GET");
// route.method has type string, not "GET"

The constraint ensures method is a string, but TypeScript widens "GET" to string during inference. The returned object loses the literal type. Discriminated unions, exhaustiveness checks, and autocomplete all depend on literal preservation. When the type widens, these features break.

Adding readonly to the constraint does not solve this. A constraint like T extends readonly string[] still widens individual elements to string. The array becomes immutable, but the element types lose their literals. Teams often add both a constraint and a manual type assertion in the function body, creating redundant type logic.

The TypeScript 3.4 release notes document const assertions as freezing literal types on simple expressions. Applying as const to an object literal makes all properties readonly and preserves each value's literal type. When applied to an array, the result becomes a readonly tuple with literal element types. This behavior extends to function arguments when the assertion appears at the call site.

Inline as const on Function Arguments: Syntax and Mechanics

Placing as const on a function argument applies the assertion before the function receives the value. The caller freezes the type, and the function sees the narrowed result. The function signature itself does not change.

function registerHandler(event: string, callback: () => void) {
  // implementation
}

registerHandler("click" as const, () => {});

The event parameter accepts string, but the caller supplies "click" narrowed to its literal type. TypeScript infers the argument as "click", not string. If the function's implementation uses event in a discriminated union or passes it to another function expecting literals, the narrow type propagates.

This syntax works with objects, arrays, and tuples:

function processConfig(config: { mode: string; flags: string[] }) {
  // implementation
}

processConfig({
  mode: "production",
  flags: ["optimize", "minify"]
} as const);

The config parameter accepts an object with string and string[] properties. The caller passes an object with mode: "production" and flags: readonly ["optimize", "minify"]. TypeScript preserves these literal types. The function signature did not require readonly or literal constraints, yet the caller achieves the same narrowing.

TypeScript const assertion syntax comparison

The TypeScript 3.4 release notes state that const assertions apply only to simple literal expressions. Attempting to assert a computed value or conditional expression fails at compile time. The assertion must wrap the literal directly.

Developers gain flexibility by choosing where to apply as const. A function accepting configuration objects can serve callers who need strict literals and callers who prefer dynamic values. The function author writes one signature. Callers who need narrow types add the assertion. Callers who do not need it omit the assertion and pass regular values.

Real-World Scenarios: Route Configs, Event Maps, and Discriminated Unions

Route configuration functions demonstrate the pattern's value. A routing library accepts an array of route definitions. Each route has a method, path, and handler. The library's internal logic dispatches based on exact method strings like "GET" or "POST". If the method type widens to string, the dispatcher cannot narrow the union correctly.

function defineRoutes(routes: Array<{
  method: string;
  path: string;
  handler: () => void;
}>) {
  return routes;
}

const routes = defineRoutes([
  { method: "GET", path: "/users", handler: () => {} },
  { method: "POST", path: "/users", handler: () => {} }
] as const);

// routes[0].method has type "GET", not string

The function signature accepts string for method, but the caller applies as const to the array. Each route's method preserves its literal type. The dispatcher can now narrow based on route.method === "GET" without type guards.

Event maps follow the same pattern. A framework's event emitter accepts an object mapping event names to payload types. The emitter's on method uses the map to enforce that listeners receive the correct payload. If event names widen to string, the map's keys lose their discriminating power.

function createEmitter<T extends Record<string, unknown>>(events: T) {
  return {
    on<K extends keyof T>(event: K, listener: (data: T[K]) => void) {
      // implementation
    }
  };
}

const emitter = createEmitter({
  click: { x: 0, y: 0 },
  keypress: { key: "" }
} as const);

emitter.on("click", (data) => {
  // data has type { readonly x: 0; readonly y: 0 }
});

The events parameter accepts any object, but the caller applies as const. Each event name becomes a literal, and each payload preserves its exact shape. The on method's listener receives a narrowed data parameter based on the event key.

Discriminated unions in state machines rely on literal types to distinguish variants. A state reducer accepts an action with a type field. The reducer switches on action.type to handle each case. If type widens to string, the switch statement loses exhaustiveness checking.

function reducer(state: State, action: { type: string; payload?: unknown }) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "increment":
      return { ...state, count: state.count + 1 };
    case "decrement":
      return { ...state, count: state.count - 1 };
    default:
      return state;
  }
}

reducer(state, { type: "increment" } as const);

The action parameter accepts type: string, but the caller supplies type: "increment" with as const. The reducer's switch statement sees the literal type and narrows accordingly. TypeScript detects when a case is missing.

These scenarios share a common need: the function logic operates on wide types, but downstream code requires narrow literals. Encoding the narrowness in the function signature forces every caller to satisfy it. Applying as const at the call site shifts the responsibility to callers who need it.

Generic Constraints vs Inline as const: When Each One Wins

Generic constraints enforce invariants across all callers. When every invocation must satisfy a type requirement, the constraint belongs in the signature. Inline as const grants flexibility. When some callers need narrow types and others do not, the assertion belongs at the call site.

Aspect Generic Constraint Inline as const
Enforcement Mandatory for all callers Optional per call site
Signature complexity Adds type parameters and bounds No signature change
Type narrowing Preserves constraint bound only Preserves exact literals
Flexibility Uniform behavior Caller-controlled behavior
Use case Invariants required by function logic Narrowing needed by caller logic

A validation function that checks an array's contents requires a constraint. The function's implementation depends on the array being readonly to avoid mutation during validation. Every caller must pass a readonly array. The constraint enforces this.

function validate<T extends readonly unknown[]>(values: T) {
  // implementation depends on immutability
}

The constraint communicates to callers that mutation is forbidden. Attempting to pass a mutable array fails at compile time. This is a true invariant of the function's contract.

A formatting function that accepts a string does not require a constraint. The function's implementation works with any string, but some callers need to preserve the specific string literal for autocomplete or discriminated unions elsewhere. Those callers add as const.

function formatMessage(template: string) {
  return template.replace(/%s/g, "value");
}

formatMessage("User %s logged in" as const);

Generic constraints versus inline assertions comparison

The function signature accepts string because the implementation does not care about narrowness. Callers who need the literal type for other purposes add the assertion. Callers who do not need it pass a plain string.

Teams evaluate whether the narrowness benefits the function's implementation or the caller's context. If the function's logic requires it, use a constraint. If the caller's downstream code requires it, use as const at the call site. When both need it, combine them.

Combining Both: Const Type Parameters and Inline Assertions

TypeScript 5.0 introduced const type parameters with the syntax <const T>. This signals that the type parameter should infer as narrow as possible without requiring as const at the call site. The function signature requests narrow inference, but callers retain the option to override it.

function createConfig<const T>(values: T) {
  return values;
}

const config = createConfig({ mode: "production", flags: ["optimize"] });
// config has type { readonly mode: "production"; readonly flags: readonly ["optimize"] }

The <const T> parameter tells TypeScript to infer T with literal types. The caller passes a plain object without as const, yet the result preserves literals. This reverses the control: the function author requests narrow inference, and callers must opt out by explicitly widening the type.

Combining <const T> with inline as const provides granular control. A function accepting multiple parameters can request narrow inference for one parameter and allow wide inference for another. Callers apply as const to specific arguments as needed.

function defineAction<const T>(type: T, payload: unknown) {
  return { type, payload };
}

const action = defineAction("increment", { amount: 5 } as const);
// action.type has type "increment"
// action.payload has type { readonly amount: 5 }

The type parameter uses <const T> to infer narrowly. The payload parameter accepts unknown, and the caller applies as const to narrow its shape. The function signature remains concise. Callers control which parts narrow.

This combination suits APIs where some arguments always need literals and others sometimes do. A router's path parameter always needs a literal string for type-safe route matching. The handler parameter might accept a plain function or a narrowed configuration object depending on the route's needs.

function route<const P>(path: P, handler: () => void) {
  return { path, handler };
}

route("/users/:id", () => {});
// path has type "/users/:id"

The <const P> parameter ensures path always infers as a literal. Callers do not need to remember to add as const. The handler parameter stays flexible. When a caller needs to narrow the handler's configuration, they apply as const to that argument only.

Developers apply this pattern selectively. Requesting narrow inference for every parameter makes the signature rigid. Applying it to parameters where narrowness benefits the function's type safety (like path patterns or discriminated union tags) keeps the API intuitive. Callers supply as const for additional narrowing when their specific use case demands it.

Common Pitfalls: When Inline as const Breaks Inference

TypeScript's type inference engine attempts to unify the narrowed type with the function's expected parameter type. When the narrowed type contains properties or shapes the parameter type does not expect, inference fails. The compiler reports that the types are incompatible.

function processData(data: { value: number }) {
  // implementation
}

processData({ value: 42, extra: "field" } as const);
// Error: Object literal may only specify known properties

The data parameter expects an object with a value property of type number. The caller supplies an object with an additional extra property and applies as const. TypeScript narrows the object to { readonly value: 42; readonly extra: "field" }. This type does not match { value: number } because of the excess property. The function signature must explicitly allow excess properties or the caller must omit them.

Applying as const to computed values fails because the TypeScript 3.4 release notes restrict const assertions to simple literal expressions. Attempting to assert a function call or conditional expression produces a compile error.

const value = (Math.random() < 0.5 ? "a" : "b") as const;
// Error: A 'const' assertion can only be applied to a string, number, boolean, array, or object literal

The assertion must wrap the literal directly. Developers who need to narrow a computed value must assign it to a const variable first, then reference that variable. The variable declaration applies the assertion implicitly.

const value = Math.random() < 0.5 ? ("a" as const) : ("b" as const);

This syntax asserts each branch of the conditional separately. The resulting type is the union "a" | "b", which preserves both literals.

Deep nesting in object literals causes TypeScript's inference to slow down when as const applies. Large configuration objects with many nested levels can trigger performance warnings. The compiler must traverse the entire structure to apply readonly and preserve literals at every level. Teams break large objects into smaller const variables to avoid this.

const baseConfig = { mode: "production" } as const;
const flags = ["optimize", "minify"] as const;

const config = { ...baseConfig, flags };

Spreading const variables composes the final object without requiring a single assertion on a deeply nested structure. Each variable narrows independently, and the spread combines them. This approach scales better than applying as const to a massive literal.

Readonly properties in const-asserted objects prevent mutation but do not prevent reassignment of the object itself. A const-asserted array becomes a readonly tuple, but the variable holding that array can still be reassigned unless declared with const.

let routes = [{ method: "GET" }] as const;
routes = [{ method: "POST" }] as const; // allowed

The routes variable is mutable. The array itself is readonly, meaning you cannot push or modify elements, but reassigning the entire variable succeeds. Developers who need true immutability declare the variable with const in addition to applying as const to the value.

Understanding these pitfalls helps teams apply inline as const correctly. The pattern works when the narrowed type remains compatible with the function's parameter type, when the assertion applies to a simple literal, and when performance remains acceptable. When these conditions hold, inline as const provides type narrowing without signature complexity.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should a function signature use a generic constraint instead of expecting callers to apply as const?

When the function's implementation depends on a type property that every caller must satisfy, encode it as a generic constraint. A validation function that iterates over a readonly array needs the constraint T extends readonly unknown[] because mutation during iteration breaks the logic. When the function works with both wide and narrow types and only some callers need narrowness, omit the constraint and let callers apply as const as needed.

Does applying as const to a function argument change the runtime behavior?

No. Const assertions are a compile-time type annotation. The TypeScript 3.4 release notes clarify that as const signals to the compiler that literal types should not widen. The compiled JavaScript code is identical to code without the assertion. The difference is purely in the type information TypeScript tracks.

Can inline as const preserve literal types through multiple function calls?

Yes, as long as each function in the chain preserves the type. If the first function returns the narrowed value and the second function accepts it without widening, the literals propagate. Breaking the chain happens when an intermediate function's return type widens the value. Generic type parameters that preserve the input type (like <T>(value: T) => T) maintain the chain.

What is the difference between const type parameters in TypeScript 5.0 and inline as const?

Const type parameters (<const T>) request narrow inference at the function signature level, applying to all callers by default. Inline as const applies at the call site, giving each caller control over whether to narrow. Combining both allows the function to request narrow inference for specific parameters while letting callers selectively narrow others with inline assertions.

Does as const work with rest parameters or variadic tuple types?

Yes. Applying as const to an array passed as a rest parameter narrows it to a readonly tuple. The function signature must accept the tuple type, either through a generic constraint or by declaring the rest parameter with readonly. When the function expects ...args: unknown[], passing ...[1, 2, 3] as const preserves the tuple type readonly [1, 2, 3].

Choosing the Right Pattern for 2026

Inline as const on function arguments shifts type narrowing control from the function signature to the call site. Function authors write simpler signatures that accept wide types. Callers who need literal preservation add the assertion. Callers who prefer flexibility omit it. This pattern reduces signature complexity while maintaining type safety for callers who need it.

Generic constraints still enforce invariants when every caller must satisfy a type requirement. Combining const type parameters with inline assertions provides granular control, allowing function authors to request narrow inference for some parameters while leaving others flexible. Teams evaluate whether narrowness benefits the function's logic or the caller's downstream code, then apply the appropriate pattern. When the function's implementation requires narrow types, use a constraint. When only some callers need them, use inline as const at the call site.

Understanding when inference breaks (excess properties, computed values, deep nesting) prevents runtime surprises and keeps compile times manageable. As TypeScript's inference engine evolves, inline as const remains a low-overhead pattern for preserving literal types without encoding every requirement in the function signature.
